stories.headline: Michigan Rep. Haley Stevens, a Democrat, endorses Republican Mike Rogers for Senate
stories.summary: Rep. Haley Stevens, who lost August's Democratic Senate primary in Michigan to Abdul El-Sayed, endorsed Republican nominee Mike Rogers on Sunday, two days before the midterms. Democrats criticized the move, and some of her staff reportedly quit. President Trump praised her at a rally.
stories.why_it_matters: Michigan is one of the closest Senate races, and Senate control may turn on a handful of contests like it. A split among Democrats this late can affect turnout and the vote count on Tuesday.
stories.background: Michigan's Senate seat is open and is one of the most closely watched races of the 2026 midterms, which will decide control of Congress. Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive, narrowly beat Rep. Haley Stevens in the August Democratic primary. Mike Rogers is the Republican nominee backed by President Trump. Tensions between progressive and moderate Democrats, including over an outside ad Stevens called antisemitic, were already running high before Sunday.

facts.text: Stevens, who lost the Democratic primary to El-Sayed, endorsed Republican Mike Rogers on Sunday, two days before Election Day.
NBC News reported the endorsement came after El-Sayed's campaign asked Stevens to stop attending campaign events over an outside ad that Stevens said was antisemitic.
PBS reported she had been uninvited from a joint event with El-Sayed the same day.
Stevens said on Sunday night that El-Sayed had been 'getting angrier and angrier' and that recent campaign ads motivated her decision, per the Washington Examiner.
The Guardian reported that her chief of staff, Justin German, and communications director, Logan Basch, were among staff who reportedly quit after the endorsement.
The Guardian reported that Trump praised the switch; at an Iowa rally he said he would like Stevens to switch parties.
Commentator James Carville, a Democrat, was reported by the New York Post to have made a vulgar remark about Stevens.

framing.note: Quotes Democrats calling it a 'despicable betrayal' and leads with the party's backlash.
Leads with Stevens defending the move as a broader point about her party.
Centers on Carville's vulgar remark rather than the race itself.

stories.headline: Judge dismisses DOJ suit over two Dan Sullivans on Alaska's Senate ballot
stories.summary: A federal judge on Sunday dismissed a Justice Department lawsuit that sought to block certification of Alaska's Senate race if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses. CNBC and Fox News report the DOJ plans to appeal. Sullivan has said he would accept the result.
stories.why_it_matters: The case tested whether the federal government can step in before votes are counted to contest a state's election result. How Alaska's race is certified affects who holds a Senate seat that could decide control of the chamber.
stories.background: Alaska's Senate race pits incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan against Democrat Mary Peltola. A second candidate, Daniel J. Sullivan, also appears on the ballot with no party affiliation. The Justice Department sued, arguing the second name could divert voters and benefit the Democrat. Alaska officials, the Peltola campaign and Democratic groups asked the court to toss the case, arguing the department lacks standing and that the ballot distinguishes the two candidates.

facts.text: A federal judge dismissed the Justice Department's lawsuit on Sunday; it had sought to block certification if Sullivan loses.
CNBC and Fox News reported the Justice Department said it would appeal.
The department had argued the second Sullivan's name on the ballot potentially diverted voters and would benefit the Democrat.

Before the ruling, Alaska's Department of Law argued the federal government has no standing and the complaint fails to state a claim under the National Voter Registration Act; it also said the second candidate is listed as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., with no party.
Sullivan said he would accept Alaska's results, while also suggesting the election could be 'stolen,' per the New York Times.
AP reported the FBI has been visiting residents of Petersburg, Alaska, where the second Sullivan lives, and that he could not be located.

framing.note: Calls it the 'latest defeat for the Trump administration,' stressing the string of losses.
Uses the nickname 'Decoy Dan' and leads with the DOJ's plan to appeal.
Headline stresses the judge's appointing president and says the case failed on procedure, not on the confusion argument.

stories.headline: Learjet crashes in Palm Beach County, Florida, killing all nine aboard
stories.summary: A Learjet flying from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas crashed Sunday in a Palm Beach County neighborhood near a busy road, killing all nine on board, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said. The cause has not been released.
stories.why_it_matters: Federal investigators will look at what caused the plane to dive, which can lead to safety changes for private jets. Residents near the site were affected by the crash and fire.
stories.background: Business jets like the Learjet fly regularly between Texas and the Bahamas. Plane crashes are investigated by the National Transportation Safety Board, with the FAA assisting. Findings usually take months, though preliminary information can come out within weeks.

facts.text: All nine people on board were killed, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said; the plane left Austin-Bergstrom International Airport headed for the Bahamas.
The crash was near a busy road in a residential area and left a large crater, per Deutsche Welle.
The New York Times reported a pilot said by radio the plane was descending at 20,000 feet per minute.
CBS News reported details about the cause had not been shared.

stories.headline: Judge dismisses Trump's $10 billion defamation suit against Wall Street Journal over Epstein letter
stories.summary: A federal judge on Saturday threw out, with prejudice, President Trump's suit against the Wall Street Journal and Rupert Murdoch over a 2025 story on a birthday letter to Jeffrey Epstein. NPR quotes the judge calling the suit 'grasping at straws.' Trump's side said it will keep pressing.
stories.why_it_matters: The ruling is a press-freedom decision: it bears on how easily public figures can sue news outlets over reporting on them.
stories.background: In July 2025 the Wall Street Journal reported that a birthday book for Jeffrey Epstein included a letter attributed to Trump. Trump denied writing it and sued for $10 billion. A dismissal with prejudice generally bars refiling the same claims, though it can be appealed.

facts.text: The judge dismissed the suit with prejudice on Saturday.
Trump denied writing the letter, which was the subject of the Journal's 2025 article.

stories.headline: Iran and US trade threats of renewed war as Doha talks end without a deal
stories.summary: President Trump told a campaign rally on Sunday he may yet have to give Iran "the hammer", and Iran replied that a new war could outlast the last one. Iranian negotiators left Doha after three days of Qatar-mediated talks, with a draft proposal for a US deal reportedly circulating. Gulf officials are said to be bracing for escalation after the US midterms on November 3.
stories.why_it_matters: A return to fighting would put at risk shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and Gulf security, and would push fuel costs up for businesses and travelers worldwide.
stories.background: The US and Israel fought a war with Iran earlier this year, and the sides have since been in a fragile pause with repeated threats to resume strikes. Qatar has been mediating indirect talks, including over the release of about $6 billion in Iranian assets that could lead to the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. Trump had previously said he would not strike Iran again before the US midterm elections. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is reported to favor resuming the campaign after the vote.

facts.text: Trump told a campaign rally on Sunday that he may have to give Iran "the hammer" at some unspecified time, reiterating a threat to resume strikes.
Iran said a renewed war with the US could last longer than the previous round and threatened retaliation without geographical limits.
Iran's supreme leader on October 31 warned the US and Israel against launching new attacks, and Secretary of State Rubio said Washington had not yet decided on new strikes.
Iranian negotiators had held a third day of indirect talks in Doha with Qatari mediators; Qatar was trying to negotiate release of $6 billion in Iranian assets.
By Monday, a Reuters report said the Iranians had left Doha and a draft proposal for a US deal was being circulated, according to an official.
Axios, citing one Israeli and one US source, reported that Trump and Netanyahu had a candid call on Saturday in which Netanyahu pressed to resume strikes; Trump later called it a good talk.
Iran said the "ball is in the U.S. court" on any deal, according to CBS News.
Diplomats told the Financial Times that renewed conflict would be more damaging to the Gulf than earlier rounds.

framing.note: Ties Trump's threat to the midterm campaign and his earlier pledge not to strike before the vote.
Headline puts Netanyahu's push for strikes alongside Trump's threat, casting Israel as the driver.

stories.headline: Localized Kherson ceasefire ends after hundreds of civilians evacuate Oleshky
stories.summary: A several-day local truce around the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in Ukraine's Kherson region has ended. It let hundreds of civilians leave a riverside area described as a kill zone. Ukraine says Russia used the pause to reinforce its positions.
stories.why_it_matters: It shows how little safe passage civilians in front-line areas have, and that even short truces are being contested.
stories.background: Russia has occupied parts of Kherson Oblast, including Oleshky on the left bank of the Dnipro River, since the 2022 invasion. Civilians remaining along the river face drone attacks from both sides of the line. The truce was a narrow, local arrangement rather than a wider ceasefire.

facts.text: Ukraine's General Staff said 167 Kherson Oblast residents trapped on the right bank of the Dnipro were evacuated, including 22 children and 21 people with limited mobility.
NPR reported the ceasefire lasted several days and allowed hundreds of residents to evacuate before it ended.
Evacuees from Oleshky reached Ukraine's Chernihiv region on Saturday after traveling through Russia and Belarus.
Reuters reported that Ukraine said Russia used the Oleshky ceasefire to reinforce positions.
AP reported that residents of Kherson are preparing for attacks as the truce ends.

stories.headline: Binance reopens withdrawals after record $6.3 billion hack; users pull billions
stories.summary: Binance went back online Sunday after a theft of about $6.3 billion that the FBI links to North Korea. Customers withdrew billions in the first hours. The exchange says withdrawals are stabilizing and it has pledged to reimburse users whose assets were stolen.
stories.why_it_matters: Anyone holding money on a crypto exchange is exposed to this kind of loss, and the size of the outflow shows how fast confidence can move.
stories.background: Binance is the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange. It froze deposits and withdrawals after the theft last week. Blockchain-analysis firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis attribute the hack to North Korea's TraderTraitor group, and the FBI has said it is working with partners on the investigation. Binance said it would cover losses.

facts.text: Customers pulled $3.64 billion, or 2.1% of Binance's assets, as the exchange went back online on Sunday, Reuters reported.
Binance said withdrawals were stabilizing after an initial spike and that deposit volumes remained "substantial".
The Wall Street Journal reported Binance says it has replaced roughly 95% of the stolen assets so far.
The hackers were linked by the FBI to North Korea; the Financial Times reported Binance pledged to reimburse users whose assets were stolen.

Blockchain intelligence firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis assessed with high confidence that North Korea's TraderTraitor group was responsible, and Binance has not independently confirmed that attribution.

stories.headline: Iliana Iotova wins Bulgaria's presidential runoff, becoming first elected female president
stories.summary: Bulgaria's acting President Iliana Iotova, an ally of Prime Minister Rumen Radev, won the Sunday runoff over banker Andrey Gyurov. Near-final results from the election commission showed her winning amid low turnout. She favors dialogue with Moscow and opposes military aid to Ukraine.

stories.background: Bulgaria's presidency is largely ceremonial but the president can influence foreign policy messaging and appoints caretaker governments. Iotova had been acting president. stories.headline: India's opposition rallies in Delhi demanding election chief's resignation
stories.summary: Thousands joined an opposition rally in New Delhi calling for the chief election commissioner to step down, over a revision of electoral rolls. It was the latest protest against Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government.
stories.why_it_matters: Voter-roll accuracy decides who can vote in the world's largest democracy.
stories.background: India's election commission has been revising voter rolls. Opposition parties say the revision is controversial and have repeatedly called for the election chief to resign. The commission's own response is not in the summaries reviewed here.

stories.headline: UN peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara ends after 35 years
stories.summary: The UN's mission in Western Sahara ceased operations Sunday after the Security Council failed to renew its mandate, the UN chief said. AP reported the lapse followed a US-Russia standoff.
stories.why_it_matters: The mission monitored a ceasefire in a disputed territory; without it, there is less independent oversight there.
stories.background: Western Sahara was once ruled by Spain and is claimed by both Morocco and the pro-independence Polisario Front. The UN mission was established 35 years ago. Council renewals have usually been annual.

facts.text: The mission will end after the Security Council failed to renew its mandate, the UN chief said Sunday.
AP and NPR reported operations ceased Sunday after 35 years; AP attributed it to a US-Russia standoff.
The territory is claimed by both Morocco and the Polisario Front.

stories.headline: Commonwealth leaders gather in Antigua amid global political turbulence
stories.summary: Leaders representing nearly a third of the world's population are meeting in Antigua this week to strengthen ties. Only left-leaning outlets in the digest covered it.
stories.why_it_matters: The meeting sets out cooperation among 50-plus countries on trade and climate, though it rarely changes daily life directly.
stories.background: The Commonwealth is a voluntary grouping of mostly former British territories. Its leaders meet every two years or so. This year's host is the Caribbean island nation of Antigua and Barbuda.

facts.text: Dozens of Commonwealth leaders are meeting in Antigua this week, representing nearly a third of the world's population.

stories.headline: US stock futures rise as oil falls, easing last week's tech selloff
stories.summary: US stock futures rose Monday and Treasury yields eased after a tech-led selloff last week, with falling oil prices cited as the main support. Outlets describe investors as returning to risk cautiously, with volatility still expected around the midterm elections and this week's economic data.
stories.why_it_matters: Retirement and investment accounts with large tech holdings swung with the AI trade last week, and outlets say further swings are possible this week. Falling oil and yields, if they hold, ease pressure on fuel prices and borrowing costs.
stories.background: Technology and artificial-intelligence stocks have driven much of the US market's gains, and trillions of dollars are tied up in that trade. Late last month tech shares sold off sharply. Separately, a conflict involving Iran has disrupted Gulf oil exports for months, keeping energy prices and inflation worries elevated. Markets are now looking ahead to the US midterm elections and monthly jobs data later this week.

The New York Times said investors are bracing for more market volatility after the tech selloff, even as futures rose Monday.
The Wall Street Journal reported investors, traders and some tech executives are seeking insurance-type protection against losses in the AI trade.
Reuters headlined that Wall Street futures rose as AI stocks 'catch their breath', with the midterms in focus.

Bloomberg reported UBS's Gerry Fowler said the market is pricing a shorter AI cycle than is likely to play out.

framing.note: Emphasizes a cautious return to risk, driven by lower oil and yields.

stories.headline: Oil drops below $100 as US and Iran pursue talks; OPEC+ holds output steady
stories.summary: US crude fell below $100 a barrel on Monday after reports that the US and Iran are pursuing diplomacy, per CNBC and the Wall Street Journal. OPEC+ kept its December output targets unchanged on Sunday, Reuters reported.
stories.why_it_matters: Oil prices feed into gasoline, shipping and food costs, so a sustained drop would ease inflation pressure; a breakdown in talks could push prices back up.
stories.background: A war involving Iran has run for roughly nine months and has disrupted Gulf oil exports. That has kept oil prices high and raised inflation concerns in fuel-importing countries. OPEC+, the producer group led by Saudi Arabia and Russia, sets output targets, though many Gulf members are producing well below them. Peace-talk reports have recently moved prices sharply.

facts.text: CNBC reported US crude fell below $100 on Monday on news that both the US and Iran are pursuing diplomacy.
The Wall Street Journal reported oil dropped amid diplomatic efforts to revive peace negotiations between Washington and Tehran.
OPEC+ kept December oil output targets steady ahead of a tougher call for 2027, per Reuters; the New York Post carried the same report, noting most Gulf members are still pumping well below targets.
MarketWatch reported Goldman Sachs analysts see Brent averaging $130 next year, and potentially reaching $140 if Middle East tensions worsen.
Bloomberg reported Indian bonds had their best day in six months as crude extended losses, easing inflation concerns.

framing.note: Headline puts the price level and the US-Iran diplomacy first.

stories.headline: Bond yields ease as investors wait on midterms, Treasury refunding and jobs data
stories.summary: US and European government bond yields fell Monday as oil prices dropped, the Wall Street Journal reported. Outlets say investors are focused on the midterm elections, the Treasury's quarterly refunding announcement and monthly employment data.
stories.why_it_matters: Treasury yields influence mortgage and loan rates, and this week's data and election outcome could move them.
stories.background: A Treasury yield is the return investors demand to lend to the government, and it helps set borrowing costs across the economy. Yields move with inflation expectations, Federal Reserve policy and government borrowing needs. The Treasury announces its borrowing plans each quarter in a refunding statement. The midterm elections will decide control of Congress, which affects spending and regulation.

facts.text: The Wall Street Journal reported US Treasury and European bond yields fell as oil prices dropped, with investors focused on midterms, the quarterly refunding and employment data.

stories.headline: Hochul campaigns with Mamdani and Ocasio-Cortez as early voting ends; Blakeman works Long Island and upstate
stories.summary: On the last day of early voting, Gov. Kathy Hochul campaigned in Democratic New York City neighborhoods alongside Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. Her Republican opponent, Bruce Blakeman, spent the weekend on Long Island and upstate. The governor's election is Tuesday.
stories.why_it_matters: New Yorkers choose a governor on Tuesday, and the weekend schedules show each campaign leaning on a different base: city Democrats for Hochul, suburban and upstate voters for Blakeman.
stories.background: Hochul, a Democrat, is seeking a full term as governor. Blakeman, the Republican nominee, is the Nassau County executive. Mamdani became mayor in January 2026 and is a prominent figure on the left of the Democratic Party, as is Ocasio-Cortez. Early voting in New York runs for nine days before Election Day, which is Tuesday, Nov. 3.

facts.text: Hochul appeared with Mamdani and Ocasio-Cortez in New York City on Sunday, including at a Buffalo Bills watch party at a bar, according to the Post and City & State.
Sunday was the last day of early voting, City & State reported.
Blakeman campaigned on Long Island and upstate, per the Times and City & State.
The Post reported that Hochul said the support of the two left-leaning figures would not turn off moderate voters.
The Post reported Blakeman began an eight-city tour of New York in 48 hours, quoting him: "We are leaving no stone left unturned."
Blakeman, with a Queens Democrat, accused Hochul of going "wok" against Asian families over a state gas-stove ban in new housing, the Post reported.

stories.headline: Police search for attacker after Brooklyn jogger stabbed on waterfront path
stories.summary: A 28-year-old woman, identified by amNY and the Times as Katie Suarez, was stabbed while running along the Brooklyn waterfront on Friday evening. The Times reports she is on life support. NYPD detectives had not identified a suspect as of Sunday.
stories.why_it_matters: A random-seeming attack on a popular running path in marathon week raises safety questions for people who exercise along the waterfront, while police have no suspect yet.
stories.background: The attack happened Friday on a path along Brooklyn's Shore Parkway, according to Fox News. Suarez was training for the New York City Marathon, which was held Sunday, amNY reported. The New York Post noted similarities that Phil Vetrano, whose daughter Karina was killed while running in Queens in 2016, saw with his own family's case.

stories.headline: Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac tighten mortgage rules for rent-regulated buildings after Mamdani's rent freeze
stories.summary: THE CITY reports that Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, the two federally backed mortgage buyers, have imposed new rules for New York City rent-regulated buildings after the mayor's rent freeze. The outlet says the rules make it very hard or impossible for some landlords to get financing. No other outlet in the digest covers it.
stories.why_it_matters: If landlords of rent-stabilized buildings cannot refinance or borrow, it could affect building upkeep and sales, which matters to the roughly one million stabilized tenants and to owners.
stories.background: Mayor Zohran Mamdani took office in January 2026 and has pushed to freeze rents on rent-stabilized apartments. Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac buy a large share of multifamily mortgages, so their underwriting rules shape what lenders will offer. Landlord groups have long argued rent limits squeeze building income.

facts.text: THE CITY reports Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac imposed new rules for rent-regulated New York City buildings after the rent freeze.
Per THE CITY's reporting, the rules make it impossible or extremely difficult for landlords to get financing.

refs.title: Government-Backed Lenders Tighten Mortgage Rules in Response to Mamdani’s Rent Freeze

stories.headline: Mamdani threatens legal action over ICE use of city parking lots
stories.summary: The Times reports that Mayor Mamdani is threatening legal action to stop Immigration and Customs Enforcement from using New York City parking lots. Earlier this year he issued an order barring ICE from using city property as staging areas. Only the Times in the digest covers it today.
stories.why_it_matters: It sets up a possible court fight between City Hall and federal immigration enforcement over where agents can operate in neighborhoods.
stories.background: Mamdani's executive order earlier this year restricted non-city law enforcement from using city property as a base. On Oct. 16, he and more than 100 elected officials urged private garage and lot owners not to make space available to ICE, after agents reportedly staged from a private lot near a Marble Hill shooting. The city's rules cover city property only. DHS said the laws apply to city property, not private lots.

stories.headline: Budget watchdog urges MTA to cut some jobs, including crew on fully automated trains
stories.summary: Gothamist reports that the Citizens Budget Commission, a fiscal watchdog, recommends the MTA eliminate some jobs to prepare for budget problems. One suggestion is removing one crew member from trains that are fully automated.
stories.why_it_matters: Staffing changes on subways and rail could affect service and union jobs, and fare and tax decisions are tied to how the MTA closes its budget gaps.
stories.background: The Citizens Budget Commission is a nonpartisan, business-backed group that studies city and state finances. It has recommended MTA staffing changes before. Unions representing transit workers have opposed reductions in train crews, and the issue has been debated in Albany.

facts.text: A new Citizens Budget Commission report recommends eliminating MTA jobs to save money, per Gothamist.
The report suggests eliminating one crew member from fully automated trains, per Gothamist.

stories.headline: School PTA fundraising gap widens along racial lines, Gothamist finds
stories.summary: Gothamist reports that the gap in parent-teacher association money across NYC schools is growing. The average white student benefited from about $250 in PTA money last school year, more than five times what the average Black student received.
stories.why_it_matters: Private fundraising can pay for aides, programs and supplies, so differences in what PTAs raise can add to unequal school resources.
stories.background: New York City public schools are funded mainly by the city and state, but parent groups at some schools raise extra money. Critics have long said this favors schools in wealthier neighborhoods. The report comes as the city debates school segregation more broadly.

facts.text: Per Gothamist, the average white student benefited from about $250 in PTA money over the last school year.

Treasury yields also fell, which the Journal tied to lower oil prices; falling yields mean bond prices are rising. Investors are focused this week on the midterms, the Treasury's quarterly refunding and Friday's jobs data.
